analysis.one_liner: Locks in the tax law's individual tax cuts permanently, including the lower top rate and larger estate tax exemption.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three Republican cosponsors in January 2021, the bill went to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent the individual tax provisions of the 2017 tax law, most of which are scheduled to expire after 2025. It would permanently keep the lower individual rate brackets topped by a 37% rate, the doubled child tax credit, the larger standard deduction, a $10 million estate and gift tax exemption per person, and the 20% deduction for pass-through business income. It would also permanently keep the caps on the state and local tax and mortgage interest deductions, and it would permanently repeal personal exemptions and most miscellaneous itemized deductions. The bill never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and wealthy households gain the most: the bill permanently keeps the 37% top rate, the $10 million-per-person estate and gift tax exemption, the increased alternative minimum tax exemption, and the 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses like partnerships and S corporations. Families with children also gain from the permanent $2,000 child tax credit and larger standard deduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, heirs to large estates, pass-through owners

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the individual rate brackets from the 2017 law, with a top rate of 37% on income over $600,000 for joint filers.
Makes permanent the doubled child tax credit of $2,000 per child, with a $500 credit for other dependents and a refundable portion capped at $1,400.
Makes permanent the larger standard deduction of $18,800 for heads of households and $12,000 for unmarried individuals, adjusted for inflation.
Makes permanent the doubled estate and gift tax exemption, replacing a $5 million baseline with $10 million, which shelters the largest estates from tax.
Makes permanent the 20% deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as partnerships and S corporations.
Makes permanent the increased exemption amounts for the alternative minimum tax, including a $1 million phase-out threshold that shields many high-income filers.

Makes permanent several smaller individual provisions, including a higher charitable contribution deduction limit for older donors, larger ABLE account contributions for people with disabilities, tax-free treatment of student loans discharged on death or disability, and the limitation on deducting gambling losses.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury and future taxpayers bear the cost, because making provisions permanent that were set to expire removes their scheduled revenue payoff. The bill also permanently keeps the $10,000 cap on the state and local tax deduction, which raises federal taxes relative to pre-2017 law for itemizers in high-tax states, and permanently repeals the moving-expense deduction for everyone except active-duty military members.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury, future taxpayers, high-tax-state itemizers

drawbacks.text: Permanently keeps the 37% top individual rate, whose largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners.
Permanently sets the estate and gift tax exemption at $10 million per person, a benefit that only applies to the largest estates and gifts.
Makes permanent the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes, which the CRS summary notes as a limitation that raises federal tax for some itemizers, particularly in high-tax states.
Permanently repeals the deduction for personal exemptions and most miscellaneous itemized deductions, and limits the moving-expense deduction to active-duty military members only.

Because all of these provisions were scheduled to expire in 2025, making them permanent converts temporary tax cuts into a permanent reduction in federal revenue, adding to deficits over time rather than ending with the original sunset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, permanent help to middle-income families through the child tax credit and standard deduction, but its largest and most lasting benefits — the 37% top rate, the $10 million estate tax exemption, and the permanent pass-through deduction — flow to high earners and the wealthiest households, and permanence turns a temporary revenue loss into a permanent one. On balance, the distribution of benefits tilts heavily toward those at the top, and the bill offered no offsetting revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on January 28, 2021, with Senators Ernst, Braun, and Inhofe as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was the last action of any kind recorded.
The Finance Committee never held a markup or voted on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill advancing further.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the scheduled expiration of the 2017 tax law's individual provisions remained in place, avoiding a permanent revenue loss that would have disproportionately benefited high earners and large estates. Families with children also did not gain the permanence of the doubled child tax credit that the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Future taxpayers; the tax cuts stayed temporary

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 28, 2021 to make the 2017 tax law's individual provisions permanent.

for.name: 3 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sen. Ernst, Sen. Braun, Sen. Inhofe)

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote; the bill sat in the Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored, and with Democrats controlling the Senate, the Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corporations, LLCs, including law firms, real estate partnerships, and investment firms)
industries.note: The bill permanently extends the 20% deduction for qualified business income, a provision whose benefits concentrate among high-earning owners of pass-through businesses. Permanence removes the scheduled 2025 sunset, locking in the revenue cost indefinitely.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Making the $10 million-per-person estate and gift tax exemption permanent means the largest estates never face a return to the lower baseline exemption in 2026. This is a benefit with no analogue for families below that wealth threshold.
The permanent 37% top rate and enlarged alternative minimum tax exemptions deliver the largest dollar savings to the highest earners. The cost is borne broadly through reduced federal revenue.

The bill permanently keeps the reduced $750,000 cap on deductible mortgage interest and ends the deduction for home equity loan interest, which dampens the tax advantage of larger mortgages. It also keeps the TCJA's pass-through provisions, which many real estate partnerships use.

industries.industry: Families with children (as taxpayers, not an industry)
industries.note: The permanent $2,000 child tax credit and larger standard deduction would meaningfully reduce tax bills for most families with children, including many middle-income households.
